comparison: Both strongly support the critical role of C95 in FGF2 oligomerization, pore formation, and translocation. OpenEval emphasizes multiple experimental approaches (FCS, cross-linking, membrane assays), while peer reviewers explicitly affirm this as a key finding with 'clear and convincing' data. High agreement on C95's essential role.

Both support the distinct role of C77 in Na-K ATPase binding rather than oligomerization. OpenEval notes C77A does not impair oligomerization/pore formation but causes mild secretion phenotype. Peer reviewers explicitly confirm C77's role in ATPase interaction. Strong concordance on C77's functional distinction from C95.

Both address C77's role in binding to Na-K ATPase. OpenEval provides detailed BLI quantitative binding data showing C77A impairment, while peer reviewers accept this as clarifying C77's requirement for ATPase interaction. Complete agreement on this mechanistic finding.

Both support the additive effects of C77/95A double mutant. OpenEval notes the double mutant shows additive effects supporting distinct roles. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this through discussion of differential roles without challenge. Agreement on functional independence of the two cysteines.

Both support functional characterization of C95A versus C77A in various assays. OpenEval details multiple complementary approaches, while peer reviewers accept these differential behaviors as 'clear and convincing' without challenge. Strong agreement on experimental validation.

Both support membrane translocation assay findings. OpenEval includes translocation data (Figures 5-6) as part of comprehensive C95 characterization. Peer reviewers accept translocation data without concerns as part of the multi-technique approach. Agreement on functional validation.

Both support MD simulation findings on C95-C95 proximity and dimerization. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of 360° simulations with machine learning, noting some speculation. Peer reviewers praise computational work as providing 'mechanistic insights' without raising methodology concerns. Strong agreement with minor OpenEval caution on speculative aspects.

Both support 1-μs MD simulation findings on dimer structure and membrane binding. OpenEval notes detailed structural characterization but flags speculative cellular context claims. Peer reviewers accept mechanistic insights from simulations as 'clear and convincing.' Agreement on core findings with OpenEval noting appropriate presentation of hypotheses.

Perfect claim overlap (C103-C111). Both strongly support XL-MS identification of two distinct dimerization interfaces. OpenEval details experimental evidence and compatibility with MD models. Peer reviewers explicitly note this as valuable contribution 'of interest for future studies.' Complete concordance.

Perfect claim overlap (C112-C125). Both support cryo-ET structural findings and integration with AlphaFold2/MD simulations. OpenEval details methodological soundness of the integrated approach. Peer reviewers praise 'comprehensive combination' of structural biology techniques. Complete agreement on structural validation.

Both support the conclusion that disulfide bonds stabilize the dimerization interface. OpenEval cites multiple lines of evidence (ML analysis, MD, XL-MS) showing interface can form without disulfide but is stabilized by it. Peer reviewer explicitly accepts this mechanistic interpretation after initial concern. Strong concordance.

Perfect claim overlap (C136-C144). Both rate as supported/accepted but acknowledge speculative aspects. OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN, noting the model requires additional validation. Peer reviewers accept as appropriately presented proposals for future investigation. Agreement that this is plausible but not fully validated.

OpenEval marks C17-C18 hypothesis about C95-C95 dimers as signaling units as UNCERTAIN, noting it relies on prior work but lacks direct in vivo evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses this specific signaling hypothesis, though peer reviewers generally accept the dimer formation findings.

OpenEval evaluates background/context claims (C1-C48, C126-C131) as SUPPORTED, representing established knowledge from prior research. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these contextual claims, focusing instead on novel findings.

Both support discussion claims about cytoplasmic disulfide formation and broader context. OpenEval notes appropriate contextualization and distinction between findings and speculation. Peer reviewer initially concerned but explicitly states additional discussion 'alleviates my concern.' Agreement after revision addressing context.
